tool.name: Flutter
tool.tagline: Google's UI toolkit for natively compiled apps from one Dart codebase
tool.description: Flutter is an open-source UI framework that renders every pixel itself, so one Dart codebase produces fast, consistent apps for iOS, Android, web, Windows, macOS and Linux. UIs are built from composable widgets, with hot reload for instant feedback. Learn it to ship polished cross-platform mobile apps with a single team and codebase.

glossary.def: A small Dart object that describes one piece of a Flutter screen, such as some text, a button or some padding. Screens are built by nesting widgets inside each other.
The nesting of widgets that makes up a Flutter screen: one widget at the top, containing others, down to the smallest pieces.
A Flutter widget with no changing data of its own: what it shows depends only on the values passed to its constructor.
A Flutter widget paired with a State object that holds data which can change while the app runs, such as a counter's value.
The object behind a StatefulWidget that keeps its changing data and builds its widgets. Flutter keeps it alive while the widget stays in the same place on screen.
The method a State object calls to change what's on screen: it runs your change, then tells Flutter to rebuild the widget before the next frame is drawn.
The method of a Flutter widget that returns the widgets it is made of. Flutter calls it whenever the widget needs to be drawn again, possibly many times.
The object passed to a widget's build method that marks the widget's place in the tree. It is used to look up things from higher up, like the theme or the screen size.
Restarting a running Flutter app from main() with your latest code. Everything on screen resets; slower than hot reload, but it picks up every change.
How a Flutter app runs while you develop it: slower and larger than the published app, but with hot reload and inspection tools.
A way of running a Flutter app that is almost as fast as the published app but still lets you measure its speed. Start it with flutter run --profile.
The fast, compact version of a Flutter app, compiled ahead of time to machine code for publishing to users.
A program on a Mac that imitates an iPhone or iPad in a window, so you can run apps without a real device.
Flutter's set of inspection tools, opened in a browser, for looking at a running app's widget tree, layout, speed and memory use.
Google's design system: a standard look and behaviour for buttons, menus, cards and screens. Flutter includes ready-made widgets for it.
In Flutter, the app-wide set of colours and text styles that widgets read instead of choosing their own.
A short message that slides up from the bottom of the screen for a few seconds, such as 'Message sent'.
A display setting that shows light text on a dark background. Apps can follow the setting the user picked for their phone or computer.
A Flutter widget that gives one screen its standard parts: a top bar, the main content, a floating button, a side menu and a bottom bar.
A Flutter widget that places its children side by side, left to right.
A Flutter widget that places its children one below another, top to bottom.
A Flutter widget that wraps one child in a box with optional padding, margin, size, background colour, border and rounded corners.
The direction a Row or Column lines up its children: across for a Row, down for a Column. The other direction is the cross axis.
Flutter's unit of size, which looks about the same on every screen. A sharp screen uses several real pixels for each logical pixel.
How many real screen pixels make up one logical pixel on a device, such as 3.0 on many phones.
A file shipped inside a Flutter app, such as an image, a font or a data file, listed in pubspec.yaml.
The visible window of a scrolling area: the part of a long list you can see right now.
In Flutter, a helper object connected to a widget such as a text field, a scrolling list or an animation, that lets your code read and steer it. Create it once and dispose of it when done.
A State object's getter that is true while its widget is on screen. Check it after an await, before calling setState or using context.
A method Flutter calls on a State object at set moments, such as initState when it is created and dispose when it is removed for good.
Moving changing data to the nearest widget above all the widgets that need it, then passing it down to them.
One still picture of the app's screen. Flutter draws a new frame many times a second, usually 60, to show changes and motion.
In Flutter layout, the limits a parent gives a child: a minimum and maximum width and height. The child must pick its size within them.
In Flutter, one screen (or dialog) on the Navigator's stack. Opening a screen pushes a route on top; going back pops it off.
The Flutter object that keeps a stack of screens (routes): push puts a new screen on top, pop goes back to the one below.
A link, for example in an email or another app, that opens a specific screen inside an app instead of its start screen.
The Flutter team's routing package: you map paths like /item/42 to screens, so web addresses and deep links open the right screen.
The object a FutureBuilder or StreamBuilder passes to its builder: whether the work is still waiting, and its data or error once there is one.
Changing data that only one widget uses, such as whether a checkbox is ticked. setState is enough for it.
Data that many widgets on different screens need, such as the signed-in user or a shopping cart.
A Flutter widget that makes data available to every widget below it, and rebuilds the ones that use the data when it changes.
A Flutter class for data that changes: its methods update the data and then call notifyListeners() so the widgets listening to it rebuild.
A class that holds one screen's changing data and actions and prepares the data for display, so the screen's widgets only have to show it.
In app architecture, the one class the rest of the app asks for a kind of data, such as users or orders. It hides whether the data comes from a server or a saved copy.
In layout, a screen width at which the app switches to a different arrangement, such as from one column to two panes at 600 logical pixels.
A Flutter widget that keeps its child clear of the phone's camera notch, status bar and other areas the system draws over.
The long-lived object Flutter keeps behind each widget on screen. It remembers the widget's place in the tree and owns its State, while the widgets themselves are rebuilt freely.
An ID you can give a Flutter widget so Flutter can tell it apart from its siblings, keeping the right State with the right item when a list changes.
A Flutter key that is unique in the whole app. It lets code elsewhere reach a widget's State, as forms do, and keeps that State if the widget moves.
A Flutter widget, such as AnimatedContainer, that animates by itself whenever one of its values changes.
An animation you drive yourself with an AnimationController, so you can start, stop, reverse or loop it.
A Flutter object that counts from 0.0 to 1.0 over a set time, one step per frame, and can play forward, backward or repeat.
A Flutter object that turns an animation's 0-to-1 progress into the range you want, such as 0 to 200 pixels or one colour to another.
The speed profile of an animation, such as starting fast and slowing down at the end, instead of moving at a constant rate.
An object that calls a function once per frame, used to drive animations. Flutter pauses it while its widget isn't visible.
The screen's signal that it is ready for the next frame. In Flutter it is also the name of the AnimationController argument that gives it a ticker.
A Flutter widget that flies a picture or other widget from one screen to the next while you navigate, such as a thumbnail growing into a full photo.
A Flutter test that builds widgets in a hidden test environment, taps and types on them, and checks what appears, with no phone needed.
In Flutter widget tests, an object that locates widgets on the test screen, such as find.text('Save').
A test that draws a widget and compares the pixels with a saved reference image, failing if they differ.
A piece of a Flutter scrolling area that lays itself out based on how far the user has scrolled, so it can build lazily, shrink or stay pinned.
The Flutter object that does the real layout, painting and tap detection for part of the screen. Only some widgets create one.
Working out which object on screen a tap or click landed on.
Flutter's core, written in C++, beneath the Dart code you write. It runs Dart, talks to the device and turns frames into pixels.
The thread that turns each finished Flutter frame into pixels using the graphics chip, working alongside the thread that runs your Dart code.
Flutter's renderer: the part that turns each frame into drawing commands for the graphics chip. It is the default on iOS and Android.
A small program that runs on the graphics chip to work out the colour of pixels, for example to draw a smooth colour blend or a blur.
Visible stutter when an app misses frames, because a frame took longer than its time slot (about 16 ms at 60 frames a second) to build or draw.
A description of what's on screen (labels, buttons and what they do) that Flutter builds for screen readers and other accessibility tools.
Flutter's way of sending messages between your Dart code and the app's native Android or iOS code, for device features Flutter doesn't cover itself.
A Flutter plugin split into separate packages, one per platform, behind one shared Dart interface.
A package from the Flutter team that generates matching, type-checked Dart, Kotlin and Swift code for platform channels.
Foreign function interface: calling functions written in another language, such as C, directly from Dart.
A Flutter class whose paint method draws freely on a canvas, used with the CustomPaint widget for charts, gauges and custom shapes.
In Flutter, the drawing surface a painter receives, with methods to draw lines, shapes, paths, images and text.
In drawing, a smooth blend from one colour into another, used to fill a shape or background.

concepts.name: Project setup and hot reload
concepts.summary: Create a Flutter project, find your way around its folders, run it on a phone, emulator or browser, and use hot reload.
concepts.why: Seeing each change on screen within a second is what makes Flutter pleasant to work with, and knowing the project layout saves hours of confusion.
concepts.body:
Flutter is a toolkit for building apps in Dart. One set of code runs on Android phones, on iPhones, in a web browser such as Chrome, and as a desktop program. Flutter draws everything on screen itself, so the app looks the same everywhere.

Install the Flutter SDK (it includes Dart), then run `flutter doctor` in a terminal. It checks the extra tools each platform needs, such as Android Studio for Android or Xcode (Apple's developer app, Mac only) for iPhone.

`flutter create my_app` makes a new project folder:
- `lib/main.dart` — your Dart code. `main()` calls `runApp(...)` to start the app.
- `pubspec.yaml` — your packages, plus the images and fonts the app uses.
- `android/`, `ios/`, `web/`, `macos/`... — small platform projects that wrap your app for each system. You rarely touch them.
- `test/` — your tests.

`flutter run` builds the app and starts it on a target: a phone plugged into your computer, an **emulator** (a pretend Android phone running in a window on your computer), Apple's **simulator** (the same idea for iPhone, Mac only), or Chrome with `-d chrome`. `flutter devices` lists what's available. Code editors such as VS Code and Android Studio can do the same through a Flutter add-on.

While you develop, the app runs in **debug mode**, where new code can be swapped in while the app keeps running. That gives you two shortcuts:

- **Hot reload** (`r` in the terminal, or save the file in your editor): your changed code is slipped into the running app and the screen is redrawn in about a second. The page you're on and the text you typed are **kept**.
- **Hot restart** (`R`): starts the app over from `main()` with your new code, so everything resets. Use it when hot reload misses a change, such as edits to `main()` or to values set up once at startup.

Debug mode is deliberately slow. To publish, `flutter build apk` (Android), `flutter build ipa` (iPhone) or `flutter build web` compiles the whole app ahead of time into a fast, compact **release** build. To check speed, run in **profile mode** with `flutter run --profile`: nearly as fast as release, but you can still measure.

`flutter pub add <package>` adds a package from pub.dev, just like `dart pub add`.
takeaways: `main()` calls `runApp` to start your app
Hot reload keeps what's on screen; hot restart starts over
Judge speed only in profile or release builds
pitfalls: Expecting hot reload to pick up changes to `main()` or to values set once at startup — use hot restart.

quiz.q: You changed some code and want to see the result without losing the page you're on or the text you typed. What do you use?
options: A full rebuild with flutter build
quiz.explain: Hot reload slips the new code into the running app and redraws it, keeping what's on screen.

concepts.name: Widgets and StatelessWidget
concepts.summary: Build screens by nesting small widgets, write your own StatelessWidget, and learn what build and BuildContext are for.
concepts.why: In Flutter everything on screen is a widget, so this mental model underlies every other lesson.
concepts.body:
Look at any app screen: a title, some text, a button, some space between them. In Flutter each of those pieces is a **widget** — a small Dart object that describes one part of the screen. Widgets are immutable: once created, a widget never changes.

You build a screen by putting widgets inside other widgets, like boxes inside boxes. A `Scaffold` (a basic screen) contains a `Column` (things stacked top to bottom), which contains a `Text` and an `ElevatedButton`. This nesting is the **widget tree**: one widget at the top, branching down to the smallest pieces.

To make your own widget, write a class that extends **`StatelessWidget`** and override its **build method**, `build(BuildContext context)`. It returns the widgets your widget is made of. A stateless widget's look depends only on the values passed to its constructor: give it the same values and it shows the same thing.

Flutter calls `build` when the widget first appears and whenever its inputs change — possibly many times a second. So keep `build` fast, and let it only describe the screen. It shouldn't do other work such as downloading data or starting a timer; that kind of extra work is called a **side effect**.

Conventions you'll see everywhere:
- Fields are `final`, and the constructor is `const` when possible: `const Greeting({super.key, required this.name});`. The `super.key` part passes on an optional key, an ID Flutter uses to tell widgets apart; you'll meet keys later.
- A widget that holds one other widget takes it as `child:`; one that holds several takes a list as `children:`.
- When `build` gets long, move part of it into a new widget class rather than a helper method. Small classes can be `const` and redraw on their own.

`build` receives a **`BuildContext`**: the widget's position in the tree. You use it to look things up from widgets higher up, such as the app's colours and fonts with `Theme.of(context)`, or the screen size with `MediaQuery.sizeOf(context)`.

Because widgets never change, "changing" the screen means building new widgets with new values. Flutter compares the new tree with the previous one and redraws only the parts that differ, so building widgets again and again is cheap.
takeaways: Screens are trees of small, immutable widgets
A StatelessWidget's look depends only on its constructor values
Use `const` constructors and split big build methods into widget classes
pitfalls: Doing extra work such as downloading data or starting timers inside `build`, which may run many times.

quiz.q: What should a StatelessWidget's build method depend on?
options: A variable outside the widget that other code keeps changing
A counter it increases on each build
Its final fields and what it looks up through BuildContext
quiz.explain: build should depend only on the widget's own values and what it looks up through context, because Flutter can call it at any time.

concepts.name: Row, Column, Container and padding
concepts.summary: Arrange widgets on screen with Row, Column, Stack, Padding, SizedBox and Container.
concepts.why: Every screen is a combination of these few layout widgets.
concepts.body:
In Flutter, layout is done with widgets too; there's no separate styling language. You place things by wrapping them in layout widgets.

- **`Column`** puts its children one below the other; **`Row`** puts them side by side. The direction they line up in is the **main axis**: down for a Column, across for a Row. The other direction is the cross axis.
- `mainAxisAlignment` spreads children along the main axis (`start`, `center`, `spaceBetween`, `spaceEvenly`...), and `crossAxisAlignment` lines them up the other way. `mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min` makes a Row or Column only as big as its children.
- Row and Column also take `spacing:` (Flutter 3.27+) to put an equal gap between children.

- **`Padding`** adds empty space around its child: `EdgeInsets.all(8)`, `.symmetric(horizontal: 16)` or `.only(top: 4)`. Sizes are in **logical pixels**, a unit that looks about the same size on every screen, however sharp it is.
- **`SizedBox`** gives a fixed width or height; an empty `SizedBox(height: 12)` is the usual way to add a gap.
- **`Center`** and **`Align`** position a single child inside the space they have.

- **`Container`** is an all-in-one box: padding, margin (space outside), size, background colour, and rounded corners, borders and shadows through `BoxDecoration`. When you need only one of these, the specific widget is clearer.
- **`Stack`** layers children on top of each other; `Positioned` places one at a set distance from its edges, handy for a badge on a profile picture.
- **`Expanded`** inside a Row or Column makes a child take up the leftover space (more on this at the next level).

To see where each widget's edges are, open the Widget Inspector in **DevTools**: Flutter's inspection tools, which open in a browser tab from your editor or from the link `flutter run` prints. Its "Show guidelines" option draws padding and alignment on the running app.

When the children of a Row are too wide for the screen, Flutter paints yellow-and-black warning stripes on the edge that overflows. The fix is to wrap a child in `Expanded` or `Flexible`, or to make the content scroll.
takeaways: Column and Row line children up along a main axis; set main and cross alignment
Padding, SizedBox, Center and Align handle spacing and placement
Stack + Positioned layer one widget over another
pitfalls: Using Container for everything — specific widgets like Padding and SizedBox are clearer.

quiz.q: Which setting spaces a Column's children evenly from top to bottom?
quiz.explain: For a Column the main axis runs top to bottom, and spaceEvenly shares the free space equally between and around the children.

concepts.name: StatefulWidget and setState
concepts.summary: Keep data that changes in a State object, update it with setState, and set up and clean up with initState and dispose.
concepts.why: Any widget that changes when the user does something — a counter, a toggle, a like button — starts here.
concepts.body:
A stateless widget can't change by itself. But a like button must flip when tapped, and a counter must count. Data that can change while the app runs, and that affects what's on screen, is called **state**.

A **`StatefulWidget`** is split into two classes:
- The widget itself, still immutable, holding the values passed in from outside.
- A **State object** (a subclass of `State`), created by the widget's `createState()` method. It keeps the changing data in ordinary fields and has the `build` method. Flutter keeps the same State object across rebuilds, as long as the widget stays in the same place in the tree.

To change what's on screen, change the fields inside **`setState(() { ... })`**. `setState` tells Flutter "this widget needs redrawing", and Flutter calls `build` again before it draws the next **frame** — one of the still pictures, usually 60 a second, that make up the moving screen. Change a field without `setState` and the value changes but the screen doesn't.

A State object also has **lifecycle methods** that Flutter calls at set moments:
- `initState()` — once, when the State is created. Set things up here, such as objects that control a text field or an animation (call `super.initState()` first).
- `didUpdateWidget(oldWidget)` — the parent rebuilt this widget with new values; react to them here.
- `dispose()` — once, when the widget leaves the screen for good. Release what you set up and cancel timers (call `super.dispose()` last).

Inside State, `widget.someField` reads the widget's fields, and `context` is available directly. The `mounted` getter is `true` while the widget is on screen. After an `await` the user may have left that screen, so check `if (!mounted) return;` before calling `setState` or using `context`.

Keep state as low in the tree as you can: only the widget that owns it is rebuilt. When several widgets need the same data, move it up to a shared parent and pass it down (**lifting state up**); a later lesson shows ways to share state across a whole app.
takeaways: Changing data lives in a State object that survives rebuilds
Change it inside `setState` to redraw the screen
Set up in `initState`, clean up in `dispose`, check `mounted` after awaits
pitfalls: Calling `setState` after an `await` when the widget is already gone — check `mounted` first.

quiz.q: You change a field of your State object without calling setState. What happens?
options: The screen updates on the next frame anyway
The value changes but the widget isn't rebuilt, so the screen shows the old value
quiz.explain: setState is what asks Flutter to rebuild; without it the new value isn't shown until something else causes a rebuild.

concepts.name: MaterialApp, Scaffold and theming
concepts.summary: Structure screens with MaterialApp and Scaffold, and style the whole app consistently with ThemeData, ColorScheme and text themes.
concepts.why: A shared theme makes the app look professional, and lets you support dark mode and change brand colours in one place.
concepts.body:
**Material Design** is Google's design system: a standard look for buttons, menus, cards and screens. Flutter ships widgets for it, and **`MaterialApp`** is usually the widget at the top of your tree. It sets up the app's theme, its language settings and moving between screens, and shows your first screen (`home:`). `CupertinoApp` is the alternative with Apple's iOS look; most apps use Material and adjust details per platform.

**`Scaffold`** gives one screen its standard parts: a top bar (`appBar`), the main content (`body`), a round action button (`floatingActionButton`), a side menu (`drawer`) and a bottom bar (`bottomNavigationBar` / `NavigationBar`). It also shows **SnackBars**, short messages that slide up from the bottom, via `ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(...)`.

A **theme** is the app's shared set of colours and text styles. Flutter uses Material 3 by default, which can build a whole palette of matching colours from one seed colour:

```dart
theme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal)),
darkTheme: ThemeData(colorScheme: ColorScheme.fromSeed(
    seedColor: Colors.teal, brightness: Brightness.dark)),
themeMode: ThemeMode.system,
```

Widgets read the theme with `Theme.of(context)`: use `colorScheme.primary`, `colorScheme.surface` and text styles like `textTheme.headlineSmall` instead of fixed colours and font sizes. Then **dark mode** (light text on a dark background, which users can switch on in their phone settings) and a later change of brand colours work automatically.

To style one kind of widget everywhere, set its theme inside `ThemeData`, e.g. `filledButtonTheme`, `inputDecorationTheme` or `cardTheme`. To change just one part of the screen, wrap that part of the tree in `Theme(data: ..., child: ...)`, or pass a `style` to a single widget.

Custom fonts are listed in `pubspec.yaml` and set with `fontFamily` or a text theme. Users can make text bigger in their phone settings, so don't give text a fixed height that would cut it off.
takeaways: MaterialApp sets up theme and navigation; Scaffold structures one screen
Build colours with `ColorScheme.fromSeed`; support dark mode with `darkTheme`
Read colours and text styles from `Theme.of(context)`
pitfalls: Writing fixed colours throughout widgets, which breaks dark mode and rebranding.

quiz.q: Where should a widget get its primary color so that dark mode works automatically?
quiz.explain: The ColorScheme from the active theme changes with light and dark themes, so reading it adapts automatically.

concepts.name: ListView and scrolling
concepts.summary: Show scrollable content with SingleChildScrollView, ListView, ListView.builder, separators and GridView.
concepts.why: Feeds, chats, settings and search results are all lists, and building them lazily keeps apps fast.
concepts.body:
When content is taller than the screen, the user needs to scroll. Flutter has several scrolling widgets:

- **`SingleChildScrollView`** makes one child (often a `Column`) scrollable. Fine for forms and short pages, but it builds everything up front, even the parts off screen.
- **`ListView(children: [...])`** is a scrolling list of a fixed set of widgets, also all built up front.

- **`ListView.builder(itemCount: n, itemBuilder: (context, i) => ...)`** builds items lazily: only those in or near the **viewport**, the visible window onto the list. As the user scrolls, new items are built and ones far off screen are dropped, so 10,000 items cost about as much as a screenful.
- **`ListView.separated`** does the same and adds a divider widget between items.
- **`GridView.builder`** builds a grid lazily; its `gridDelegate` sets a fixed number of tiles per line (`SliverGridDelegateWithFixedCrossAxisCount`) or a maximum tile width (`...MaxCrossAxisExtent`).

`ListTile` is a ready-made list line with `leading` (an icon or picture on the left), `title`, `subtitle`, `trailing` (something on the right) and `onTap`.

To control scrolling from code, use a `ScrollController`: create it in `initState` and dispose of it in `dispose`. Listening to it tells you when the user nears the end, so you can load more. `RefreshIndicator` adds pull-down-to-refresh.

A classic error: a `ListView` directly inside a `Column`. A Column lets each child be as tall as it likes, and a list wants to be as tall as all its items, so Flutter can't settle on a height and reports "Vertical viewport was given unbounded height". Wrap the list in `Expanded` so it gets exactly the space that's left. Avoid `shrinkWrap: true` on long lists: it makes the list build every item to measure itself, which defeats lazy building.

When items can be reordered or removed, give each one a stable key such as `ValueKey(item.id)`, so Flutter keeps each item's state with the right item (a later lesson explains why).
takeaways: `ListView.builder`/`separated` build items lazily — use them for long lists
A ListView inside a Column needs `Expanded`
ListTile is the standard row; GridView.builder for grids
pitfalls: Using `shrinkWrap: true` on a long list inside another scroll view, which builds every item.

quiz.q: Why use ListView.builder for a list of 10,000 messages?
options: It builds only the items near the visible area
It is the only list that scrolls
quiz.explain: builder creates item widgets only as they scroll into view, so memory use and build time stay low.

concepts.name: Buttons, text fields and gestures
concepts.summary: Handle taps with buttons and GestureDetector, read text with TextField and TextEditingController, and use switches and checkboxes.
concepts.why: Interactive apps need input, and controllers must be set up and cleaned up correctly, or typed text gets lost and memory is wasted.
concepts.body:
**Buttons**: `FilledButton`, `ElevatedButton`, `OutlinedButton`, `TextButton` and `IconButton` take an `onPressed` callback. Pass `null` instead to show the button greyed out and disabled.

**Gestures** on any widget: wrap it in `GestureDetector` (`onTap`, `onLongPress`, `onPanUpdate` for dragging...) or in `InkWell`, which also shows Material's ripple effect when tapped.

**Text input** uses `TextField` (or `TextFormField` inside a form):
- `onChanged: (text) => ...` runs on every keystroke.
- A **`TextEditingController`** lets your code read and set the text: `controller.text`, `controller.clear()`. A **controller** is a helper object connected to a widget that your code can steer it through. Create it once in your State (in `initState` or as a field), and call its `dispose()` from your State's `dispose`, or it keeps using memory after the screen is gone.
- `decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: ..., hintText: ..., errorText: ...)` adds a label, a grey hint and an error message.
- `keyboardType` picks the on-screen keyboard (e.g. numbers only), `textInputAction` the label on its Enter key, and `obscureText` hides passwords; there are also `autofocus` and `onSubmitted`.
- A `FocusNode` controls which field has focus (receives the typing); `FocusScope.of(context).unfocus()` hides the keyboard.

**Selection controls** such as `Switch` are *controlled* widgets: `Switch(value: on, onChanged: (v) => setState(() => on = v))`, and likewise `Checkbox`, `Radio`, `Slider` and `DropdownMenu`. The widget always shows the `value` you pass in; a tap only *reports* the new value to `onChanged`. You must store it and rebuild.

When the keyboard opens, `Scaffold` shrinks its body to make room by default; put forms in a scroll view so fields aren't hidden.
takeaways: `onPressed: null` disables a button
Controllers are created in State and disposed in `dispose`
Switches, checkboxes and sliders are controlled: store the value and rebuild
pitfalls: Creating a TextEditingController inside `build`: a new one is made on every rebuild, the typed text is lost, and the old ones are never disposed.

quiz.q: A Switch's onChanged handler is `(v) {}` — what happens when the user taps it?
options: It appears not to change, because the value passed in never changes
quiz.explain: Switch is controlled: it displays the value you pass, so you must store the new value and call setState.

concepts.name: Images, icons and assets
concepts.summary: Declare assets in pubspec.yaml, show local and network images, and use icons and resolution-aware variants.
concepts.why: Logos, illustrations and avatars appear on almost every screen, and misconfigured assets are a common first bug.
concepts.body:
Files that ship inside your app — images, fonts, data files such as a list of countries — are called **assets**. You list them in `pubspec.yaml`:

```yaml
flutter:
  assets:
    - assets/images/
    - assets/data/countries.json
```

Listing a folder includes the files in it, but not the files in folders inside it. After editing `pubspec.yaml`, stop the app and run it again; hot reload doesn't pick up new assets.

Showing images:
- `Image.asset('assets/images/logo.png', width: 120)` shows a bundled image.
- `Image.network(url, fit: BoxFit.cover, loadingBuilder: ..., errorBuilder: ...)` downloads an image from a web address and shows it. Always give it an `errorBuilder`, a widget to show instead if the download fails.
- `fit` controls how the image fills its box: `cover` fills it and crops, `contain` fits all of it inside, `fill` stretches it.
- `CircleAvatar(backgroundImage: NetworkImage(url))` makes a round profile picture.

The `cached_network_image` package keeps downloaded images saved on the phone, so they aren't downloaded again next time.

**Resolution variants**: phone screens differ in sharpness, that is in how many real pixels make up one logical pixel (the **device pixel ratio**). Put `2.0x/logo.png` and `3.0x/logo.png` next to `logo.png`, and Flutter picks the best one for each device.

**Icons**: `Icon(Icons.home)` draws one of the Material icons that come with Flutter; the `cupertino_icons` package has iOS-style ones. SVG images (a format that stays sharp at any size) need the `flutter_svg` package.

Read a text asset with `await rootBundle.loadString('assets/data/countries.json')` (from `package:flutter/services.dart`).

A big photo takes a lot of memory once it's unpacked for display. For small thumbnails, pass `cacheWidth`/`cacheHeight` so Flutter unpacks it at the size you actually show.
takeaways: Declare assets in `pubspec.yaml`, then restart the app
Always give network images an `errorBuilder`
Use 2.0x/3.0x variants and `cacheWidth` for sharp, memory-friendly images
pitfalls: Forgetting to list the asset folder in `pubspec.yaml`, causing "Unable to load asset".

quiz.q: You added assets/images/ to pubspec.yaml, but files in assets/images/icons/ aren't found. Why?
options: Listing a directory doesn't include its subdirectories
quiz.explain: Each subdirectory must be listed separately in the assets section.

concepts.name: Constraints, Expanded and Flexible
concepts.summary: Understand Flutter's rule that constraints go down, sizes go up and parents set position, and fix overflow and unbounded errors.
concepts.why: Almost every confusing layout bug is explained by the constraint model.
concepts.body:
Flutter layout follows one rule: **constraints go down, sizes go up, parent sets position**. **Constraints** are the limits a parent gives a child: a minimum and maximum width, and a minimum and maximum height.

1. A parent passes each child its constraints.
2. The child picks its own size within those limits and reports it up.
3. The parent decides where to place the child.

Consequences:
- A widget can't choose any size it wants, only one inside its constraints. Constraints are **tight** when minimum and maximum are equal, so there's no choice at all. `Container(width: 100)` used as the whole screen still fills the screen, because the screen gives tight constraints. Wrap it in `Center` or `Align`, which loosen them (minimum zero).
- A widget doesn't know its position, and can't size itself relative to the screen without being told.

In a Row or Column, children that aren't flexible get **unbounded** space along the main axis (a maximum of infinity): they're asked how big they'd like to be. Then:
- **`Expanded(child: ...)`** forces the child to fill the leftover space, shared out by `flex` factors.
- **`Flexible(child: ...)`** lets the child be *at most* its share (`FlexFit.loose`).
- Text that would overflow a Row should sit in `Expanded` or `Flexible` with `overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis`.

Errors decoded:
- "RenderFlex overflowed by N pixels" — RenderFlex is the layout object behind every Row and Column; its children are bigger than it is. Make one child flexible, or make the content scroll.
- "Viewport was given unbounded height" — a scrolling list inside a Column; give it a bounded height with `Expanded` or `SizedBox`.
- "BoxConstraints forces an infinite width" — a widget that wants to be infinitely wide inside a parent with no width limit.

`LayoutBuilder` hands you the incoming constraints so you can choose a layout from the space available.
takeaways: Constraints go down, sizes go up, the parent positions
Expanded fills leftover space by `flex`; Flexible may be smaller
Center/Align loosen tight constraints so explicit sizes apply
pitfalls: Fixing overflow by hard-coding widths, which breaks on other screen sizes.

quiz.q: Why does `Container(width: 100, height: 100, color: Colors.red)` as the app's root fill the whole screen?
options: The screen passes tight constraints, so the child must be exactly screen-sized
It's a bug in debug mode
quiz.explain: The root receives tight constraints equal to the screen; the child can only choose a size within them.

concepts.name: Navigation and routing
concepts.summary: Move between screens with Navigator push and pop, pass data both ways, and use go_router when screens need their own web addresses.
concepts.why: Every app with more than one screen needs navigation, and web addresses and links into the app need a router that maps addresses to screens.
concepts.body:
Each screen you can go to is a **route**. The **`Navigator`** keeps routes in a stack, like a pile of cards: the top card is what you see, and going back removes it.

- `Navigator.push(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => DetailScreen(id: 3)))` shows a new screen; data for it is just constructor arguments.
- `Navigator.pop(context, result)` goes back to the previous screen, optionally handing back a value. `push` returns a `Future` that completes with that value, so `final picked = await Navigator.push(...)` works for picker screens.
- `pushReplacement` swaps the current screen (e.g. after login); `pushAndRemoveUntil` removes the screens below as well.
- `showDialog` and `showModalBottomSheet` (a panel that slides up from the bottom) also push routes and return futures.

Calling `push` and `pop` yourself is the step-by-step, **imperative** style, and it's fine for simple apps. It struggles with **deep links** (a link in an email or another app that opens a specific screen of yours), the address bar on the web, and tabs that each keep their own back history. For those, use a **router**: you describe which screen belongs to which address, and it sets up the screens for you. Describing the result instead of the steps is called the **declarative** style. The Flutter team maintains **`go_router`**:

```dart
final router = GoRouter(routes: [
  GoRoute(path: '/', builder: (c, s) => const HomeScreen()),
  GoRoute(path: '/item/:id', builder: (c, s) =>
      ItemScreen(id: s.pathParameters['id']!)),
]);
MaterialApp.router(routerConfig: router);
```

Each route gets a path such as `/item/42`, like the end of a web address. Navigate with `context.go('/item/42')` (replace the screens to match that path) or `context.push('/item/42')` (add on top). A `redirect` function can send users who aren't logged in to the login screen, and `StatefulShellRoute` keeps a separate stack per tab.

On Android, `PopScope` lets you catch the system back gesture, e.g. to ask "Discard this draft?". After awaiting a pushed route, check `context.mounted` before using `context` again.
takeaways: `push` returns a Future completed by `pop(context, result)`
Pass data to screens through constructor arguments
Use go_router for web addresses, deep links, login checks and tab stacks
pitfalls: Using `context` after awaiting a route without checking `context.mounted`.

quiz.q: What does `await Navigator.push(...)` return?
options: The value passed to Navigator.pop for that route (or null)
quiz.explain: push returns a Future that completes with the result given to pop when that route is closed.

concepts.name: Forms and validation
concepts.summary: Group fields in a Form, check them with validator functions, and submit only valid data.
concepts.why: Sign-up, checkout and settings screens all need checked input with clear error messages.
concepts.body:
A **`Form`** groups `TextFormField`s (and other form fields) so you can check and save them together. To reach the form from a button, give it a **`GlobalKey<FormState>`**: a key you create once and keep in your State object, whose `currentState` gives you the form's own State.

Checking input is called **validation**. Each `TextFormField` takes a `validator`: a function that receives the current text (`String?`) and returns an error message, or `null` when the value is fine. On submit:

```dart
if (_formKey.currentState!.validate()) {
  _formKey.currentState!.save();
  // send data
}
```

`validate()` runs every validator, shows the messages under the fields and returns whether all passed. `save()` then calls each field's `onSaved` callback, which copies the value into your own variables.

Details that make forms pleasant:
- `autovalidateMode: AutovalidateMode.onUserInteraction` checks each field as soon as the user has edited it, instead of only on submit.
- `keyboardType: TextInputType.emailAddress` shows a keyboard with @, `textInputAction: TextInputAction.next` jumps to the next field, and `autofillHints` lets the phone fill in saved details.
- While the data is being sent, disable the submit button and show progress.

Some errors only the **server** can spot — the computer your app sends the data to, which might reply "email already taken". Store that message in state and return it from the validator, or show it with `InputDecoration.errorText`.

Keep validation logic in plain Dart functions: they are easy to check with small automated tests (**unit tests**). Wrap the form in a `SingleChildScrollView` so the keyboard doesn't hide fields.
takeaways: A GlobalKey<FormState> lets you call validate() and save()
Validators return an error message or null
Keep validation in plain functions you can unit test
pitfalls: Creating the GlobalKey inside `build`, which makes a new form state on every rebuild.

quiz.q: What should a TextFormField validator return when the input is valid?
quiz.explain: Returning null means no error; any string is shown as the error message.

concepts.name: FutureBuilder and StreamBuilder
concepts.summary: Show loading, data and error states for asynchronous work with FutureBuilder and StreamBuilder, without refetching on every build.
concepts.why: Every screen that loads data must handle loading and failure gracefully.
concepts.body:
**`FutureBuilder<T>`** rebuilds when a future completes. **`StreamBuilder<T>`** does the same for a **stream**: Dart's type for a series of values that arrive over time, like new chat messages, rather than one value. Both call your `builder(context, snapshot)` with an **`AsyncSnapshot`**, which describes how the work is going:

- `snapshot.connectionState` — `none`, `waiting`, `active` (streams) or `done`.
- `snapshot.hasData` / `snapshot.data`.
- `snapshot.hasError` / `snapshot.error`.

A typical builder returns a spinner while waiting, an error message on error, and the content otherwise. Dart 3 patterns make this tidy: `switch (snapshot) { AsyncSnapshot(hasError: true) => ..., AsyncSnapshot(:final data?) => ..., _ => spinner }`.

The most common bug: creating the future **inside `build`**:

```dart
FutureBuilder(future: api.fetchUser(), ...) // refetches on every rebuild!
```

Any rebuild — a theme change, the keyboard opening, a parent calling `setState` — calls the fetch function again, starts loading all over and flashes the spinner. Instead, create the future once in `initState` (or outside the widget) and keep it in a field. To refresh, assign a new future inside `setState`.

`StreamBuilder` starts and stops listening to the stream automatically as the widget appears and disappears. Pass `initialData` to avoid a flicker when you already have a value.

In bigger apps, keep loading logic outside widgets (the state-management and architecture lessons show how) and give widgets simple states: loading, data, error. `FutureBuilder` is ideal for small, local cases.
takeaways: Handle waiting, error and data states from AsyncSnapshot
Create the future once (initState or a field), never in `build`
Refresh by assigning a new future in `setState`
pitfalls: Calling the fetch function directly in the `future:` argument, re-running it on every rebuild.

quiz.q: Why is `FutureBuilder(future: api.fetchUser(), ...)` written directly in build a bug?
options: FutureBuilder can't take futures from functions
Each rebuild starts the fetch again and resets the snapshot to waiting
quiz.explain: build runs often, so the future must be created once and reused across rebuilds.

concepts.name: HTTP requests and JSON models
concepts.summary: Fetch data from a server with package:http, turn the JSON it returns into typed Dart classes, and handle errors.
concepts.why: Nearly every app gets its data from a server, and typed model classes catch mismatches with that data early.
concepts.body:
Most apps get their data from a **server**: a computer on the internet that waits for messages and answers them.

The messages follow **HTTP**, the same rules a browser uses to load web pages. Your app sends a **request**, such as "give me the todo list", and the server sends back a **response**.

Each response carries a **status code**, a number saying how it went: 200 means OK, 404 "not found", and 500 means the server itself failed. The data usually comes as **JSON**, a text format of nested lists and key-value pairs that looks much like a Dart map literal: `{"id": 1, "title": "Buy milk"}`.

Add the official **`http`** package (`flutter pub add http`). `http.get(Uri.parse(url))` and `http.post(uri, headers: ..., body: jsonEncode(data))` return a `Future<Response>` with `statusCode` and `body`. Check the status yourself: `http` doesn't throw on 404 or 500. It only throws when the request can't get through at all, for example with no internet connection (`SocketException` or `ClientException`).

`jsonDecode(response.body)` from `dart:convert` turns the text into Dart maps and lists typed only as `Map<String, dynamic>` or `List<dynamic>`; `dynamic` means Dart won't check what's inside. So convert it straight away into **model classes**, plain Dart classes with typed fields:
- a `factory User.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json)` constructor, ideally using Dart 3 map patterns to check types: `{'id': int id, 'name': String name}`;
- a `toJson()` method for sending.

For bigger models, **code generation** packages (`json_serializable`, run by `build_runner`, or `freezed`) write these repetitive methods for you.

Good practices:
- Keep HTTP code out of widgets, in a separate class (often called a **repository**) that the rest of the app asks for data. It returns model objects and throws clear errors of its own.
- Create one `http.Client`, reuse it (it keeps connections open between requests) and `close()` it when done.
- Add a time limit: `.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 10))` fails the future if the server is too slow.
- Decoding very large JSON can freeze the screen; do it in the background with `compute` or `Isolate.run`.
- Android release builds need the `INTERNET` permission in `AndroidManifest.xml`; macOS apps need the network-client entitlement in their settings.

`dio` is a popular alternative with extras such as cancelling requests and progress reports.
takeaways: Check `statusCode` yourself — http doesn't throw on error codes like 404 or 500
Convert JSON to typed model classes straight away, e.g. with map patterns
Keep HTTP code in a repository class, not in widgets
pitfalls: Reading `json['field']` loosely all over your widgets, so a change in the server's data crashes the app far from the cause.

quiz.q: A server answers with status 500. What does `await http.get(uri)` do?
quiz.explain: package:http only throws when the request can't get through; error status codes come back as normal responses.

concepts.name: Shared state: ChangeNotifier and Provider
concepts.summary: Lift state up, share it with InheritedWidget, hold it in a ChangeNotifier, and use provider or Riverpod for app-wide state.
concepts.why: Once several screens need the same data, setState alone becomes unmanageable.
concepts.body:
`setState` is ideal for **ephemeral state**: data only one widget uses, like whether a checkbox is ticked. **App state** — the signed-in user, a shopping cart, settings — is needed by many widgets on different screens.

Step one is lifting state up: move the data to the nearest widget above all the ones that need it, and pass data and callbacks down through constructors. This works, but in a deep tree you end up passing values through many widgets that don't use them ("prop drilling").

Flutter's built-in way to hand data down without that is **`InheritedWidget`**: widgets below it look it up through `context` (usually via a static `of(context)` method) and are rebuilt automatically when it changes. `Theme.of` and `MediaQuery.of` work this way.

To hold data that changes, use a **`ChangeNotifier`**: a class that keeps data, has methods that change it, and calls `notifyListeners()` afterwards to tell whoever is listening. Widgets rebuild on those notifications with `ListenableBuilder`, or through packages:
- **provider** — a package built on InheritedWidget. Provide an object with `ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => Cart(), child: ...)`. Then `context.watch<Cart>()` reads it and rebuilds when it changes, `context.read<Cart>()` reads it without rebuilding (for button callbacks), and `context.select` rebuilds only when one chosen value changes.
- **Riverpod**, **Bloc/Cubit**, **signals** and others make different trade-offs: how easy they are to test, and how much repetitive code they need.

Flutter's official architecture guide uses ChangeNotifier-based **view models** — classes that hold one screen's data and actions — with `ListenableBuilder`. Whatever you choose, keep the app's rules and calculations out of widgets, prefer replacing data over changing it in place where practical, and rebuild as small a part of the tree as you can.
takeaways: Ephemeral state: setState; shared app state: lift it up or use a notifier
ChangeNotifier + notifyListeners tells widgets when data changes
provider: `watch`/`select` to rebuild, `read` inside callbacks
pitfalls: Calling `context.watch` inside an `onPressed` callback — use `read` there.

quiz.q: In provider, which call should an onPressed callback use to add an item to the cart?
quiz.explain: read gets the object without subscribing to changes, which is what event handlers need.

concepts.name: Responsive and adaptive layouts
concepts.summary: Adapt layouts to screen size with MediaQuery, LayoutBuilder and breakpoints, and respect safe areas, rotation and platform habits.
concepts.why: Flutter apps run on phones, tablets, foldables, desktops and the web, so one fixed layout isn't enough.
concepts.body:
**Responsive** means the layout adjusts to the space available; **adaptive** means it adjusts to the device's input and habits (mouse or touch, iOS or Android).

Tools for size:
- `MediaQuery.sizeOf(context)` — the size of the app's window. Prefer the specific methods (`sizeOf`, `paddingOf`, `orientationOf`) over `MediaQuery.of(context)`: the widget then rebuilds only when that one value changes.
- **`LayoutBuilder`** — gives the constraints from the parent, which is better for reusable pieces that may sit in a side panel rather than fill the screen.
- **Breakpoints** — widths at which you switch layout. Material 3 calls below 600 logical pixels (dp) wide compact, 600–839 medium, and 840 and up expanded. A compact layout might put a `NavigationBar` at the bottom; wider ones a `NavigationRail` (a column of icons on the left) and two side-by-side panes.

Other essentials:
- **`SafeArea`** keeps content clear of the camera notch, the status bar (clock and battery) and the swipe bar at the bottom.
- Flexible widgets (`Expanded`, `Wrap`, `GridView` with `maxCrossAxisExtent`) adapt better than fixed sizes.
- `OrientationBuilder`, or the size itself, handles rotating the phone.
- Text size: test with large fonts, and don't fix heights around text.

Adaptive touches: `Theme.of(context).platform` or `defaultTargetPlatform` to choose platform-specific behaviour, `.adaptive` constructors (`Switch.adaptive`, `CircularProgressIndicator.adaptive`) that pick the native look, and hover effects and keyboard shortcuts on desktop and web.

Don't lock the app to portrait (upright) unless there's a strong reason; Android's guidance for tablets and foldable phones discourages it.
takeaways: Use `MediaQuery.sizeOf` for window size and LayoutBuilder for local space
Switch layouts at breakpoints (e.g. 600 and 840 dp)
Wrap content in SafeArea and test large text
pitfalls: Using `MediaQuery.of(context).size` everywhere, causing rebuilds on any change such as the keyboard opening.

quiz.q: A reusable card should pick a layout based on the space its parent gives it, not the whole screen. What should it use?
quiz.explain: LayoutBuilder provides the parent's constraints, which reflect the space actually available to the widget.

concepts.name: The element tree, keys and State identity
concepts.summary: Learn how widgets map to elements, when State is kept or recreated, and how ValueKey, ObjectKey, UniqueKey and GlobalKey change that.
concepts.why: Bugs like state jumping to the wrong list item or text fields losing input come from not understanding element identity.
concepts.body:
Widgets are short-lived descriptions. Behind them Flutter keeps a long-lived **element tree**: for each widget on screen there's an **element** that remembers its place, and the element of a StatefulWidget owns its `State` object.

On rebuild, Flutter walks the old elements and the new widgets side by side. For each position it asks `Widget.canUpdate(old, new)`: **same runtime type and same key**? If so, the element is reused and updated with the new widget: the State survives and `didUpdateWidget` runs. If not, the old element (and its State) is thrown away and a new one is created.

Without keys, the children of a `Column` or `ListView` are matched **by position**. Remove the first item from a list of tiles that each have State, and the old first tile's State is now attached to what was the second item: checkboxes, text and animations appear to jump.

A **key** is an ID you attach to a widget so it's matched by identity instead:
- `ValueKey(todo.id)` — identity from a stable value; the usual choice for list items.
- `ObjectKey(obj)` — identity of one particular object.
- `UniqueKey()` — different every time, forcing a fresh State on every build (useful to reset a widget on purpose).
- `GlobalKey` — unique across the whole app; lets an element move to a new parent and keep its State, and gives access to `currentState` (as with forms). It's relatively expensive; use it sparingly.

Keys only matter among **siblings** (except GlobalKey). Also note that wrapping a widget in a new parent only sometimes (e.g. `if (x) Padding(child: w) else w`) changes the shape of the tree and recreates the State.
takeaways: Elements (and State) are reused when runtime type and key match
Unkeyed siblings are matched by position
Use ValueKey for list items; GlobalKey sparingly
pitfalls: Using `UniqueKey()` in a list item builder, which recreates every item's State on every rebuild.

quiz.q: Two widgets at the same position have the same type and key across rebuilds. What happens to the StatefulWidget's State?
options: It's moved to the end of the list
It's kept and the element is updated with the new widget
quiz.explain: canUpdate is true, so the existing element and its State are reused and didUpdateWidget is called.

concepts.name: Implicit and explicit animations
concepts.summary: Animate with implicit widgets like AnimatedContainer, build explicit animations with AnimationController and Tween, and use Hero transitions.
concepts.why: Motion makes apps feel polished and helps users follow changes, and Flutter makes it cheap to add.
concepts.body:
**Implicit animations** are the easy path: widgets such as `AnimatedContainer`, `AnimatedOpacity`, `AnimatedAlign`, `AnimatedPadding`, `AnimatedSwitcher` and `AnimatedCrossFade` animate by themselves whenever one of their values (size, colour, see-through-ness...) changes. Give them a `duration` and optionally an **animation curve**, the speed profile, such as starting fast and slowing down (`Curves.easeOut`). Then just change the values with `setState`. `TweenAnimationBuilder` does the same for any value.

**Explicit animations** give full control: looping, reversing, playing several one after another, following a finger.

- An **`AnimationController`** counts from 0.0 to 1.0 over a `duration`, one step per frame. It needs a `vsync`: something that wakes it each frame (a **ticker**) and pauses it while the widget isn't visible. Mix `SingleTickerProviderStateMixin` (or `TickerProviderStateMixin` for several controllers) into your State and pass `this`. Create the controller in `initState` and **dispose of it** in `dispose`.
- Control it with `forward()`, `reverse()`, `repeat()`, `animateTo()`, `stop()`.

- A **`Tween`** turns 0–1 into the range you want: `Tween(begin: 0.0, end: 200.0).animate(CurvedAnimation(parent: controller, curve: Curves.easeOut))`.
- Rebuild with **`AnimatedBuilder`** (or ready-made transition widgets like `FadeTransition`, `SlideTransition`, `ScaleTransition`) so only the animated part of the tree rebuilds each frame.

**Hero** flies a widget from one screen to the next as you navigate, such as a thumbnail growing into a full photo: wrap the widget on both screens in `Hero(tag: sameTag, child: ...)`.

Prefer animating opacity, position, scale and rotation: those are cheap for Flutter to draw. Respect `MediaQuery.disableAnimationsOf(context)` for users who turned on "reduce motion" in their settings.
takeaways: Implicit `Animated*` widgets animate when their values change
AnimationController + Tween + a transition or AnimatedBuilder for full control
Controllers need a TickerProvider mixin and must be disposed
pitfalls: Calling setState in an animation listener to rebuild the whole screen every frame instead of using AnimatedBuilder or a transition.

quiz.q: What does `SingleTickerProviderStateMixin` give an AnimationController?
options: A ticker that fires once per frame and pauses while the widget isn't visible
quiz.explain: The mixin makes the State a ticker provider, so the controller steps in time with frames and stops while off screen.

concepts.name: Unit, widget and integration tests
concepts.summary: Check logic with unit tests, screens with widget tests using WidgetTester and finders, and whole user journeys with integration tests.
concepts.why: Widget tests run in milliseconds without a phone and catch broken screens before users do.
takeaways: Unit tests for logic, widget tests for screens, integration tests for whole journeys
`pumpWidget`, interact, then `pump()` before checking
Find widgets by key, text, type or icon; use fakes instead of a real server
pitfalls: Forgetting `await tester.pump()` after a tap, so the expectation sees the old screen.

quiz.q: After `await tester.tap(...)` triggers setState, why call `await tester.pump()` before checking the text?
options: To draw a new frame so the rebuilt widgets are visible to finders
It's optional and has no effect
quiz.explain: The test environment only rebuilds when a frame is pumped, so pump applies the pending setState.

concepts.name: App architecture: layers, view models, DI
concepts.summary: Split an app into views, view models, repositories and services, pass dependencies in from outside, and keep data flowing one way.
concepts.why: Without clear layers, Flutter apps turn into giant widgets that are impossible to test or change.
concepts.body:
Flutter's official architecture guide splits an app into layers, each with one job.

- **UI layer** (UI = user interface, everything the user sees and touches) — **views** (widgets) show state and pass user actions on; **view models** (often `ChangeNotifier`s) hold a screen's state, offer its actions as methods, and turn data into what the view shows. Widgets contain no business logic, meaning the app's own rules, like "orders over $50 ship free".

- **Data layer** — **repositories** are the single source of truth for one kind of data (users, orders). They combine services, keep a **cache** (a saved copy, so the same data isn't fetched twice), retry failed requests, and turn raw data into the app's model classes. **Services** each wrap one outside source: a web API, a database on the phone, or a **plugin** (a package that reaches a phone feature such as the camera). Services keep no data of their own.
- Optionally a **domain layer** of "use cases", for logic that spans several repositories.

Data flows **one way**: services → repositories → view models → views. Events go the other way: the view calls a view-model method, which calls a repository, which updates state, which notifies the view.

**Dependency injection**: create services and repositories once when the app starts, and pass them into view models through their constructors, instead of letting each class create its own. Then a test can pass in fakes. `provider` (or Riverpod, `get_it`) makes these objects available to the widget tree.

Other recommendations: immutable model classes (`freezed` helps), returning a `Result` value (success or error) instead of throwing exceptions across layers, folders by feature (`lib/ui/cart/`, `lib/data/repositories/`), and **commands**: small objects that wrap an action together with its running and error state.

Scale the structure to the app — a two-screen app doesn't need use cases.
takeaways: Views + view models (UI) and repositories + services (data)
Data flows one way; events flow back through view-model methods
Pass dependencies in through constructors so layers can be faked in tests
pitfalls: Calling the server directly from widgets, which makes them hard to test and duplicates logic.

quiz.q: In the recommended architecture, which layer should cache data and be the source of truth for it?
quiz.explain: Repositories own data for their type, combining services, caching and converting to domain models.

concepts.name: Slivers and custom scroll effects
concepts.summary: Compose scrollable areas from slivers with CustomScrollView, SliverAppBar, SliverList and SliverGrid.
concepts.why: Collapsing headers, mixed lists and grids, and sticky sections all require slivers.
concepts.body:
A **sliver** is a slice of a scrolling area that lays itself out based on how far the user has scrolled, building only what's visible. `ListView` and `GridView` are convenient wrappers around a single sliver. To mix several kinds of content in one scroll, use a **`CustomScrollView`** with a list of slivers:

- **`SliverAppBar`** — a top bar that can expand and collapse (`expandedHeight`, `flexibleSpace: FlexibleSpaceBar(...)`), stay `pinned`, or reappear when scrolling up (`floating`, `snap`).
- **`SliverList`** with `SliverChildBuilderDelegate`, or the handier `SliverList.builder` / `SliverList.separated` — lazy lists.
- **`SliverGrid`** — lazy grids.
- **`SliverToBoxAdapter`** — wraps one ordinary widget. Flutter calls ordinary widgets box widgets, since they lay out as rectangles.
- **`SliverPadding`**, **`SliverFillRemaining`**, **`SliverPersistentHeader`** (custom headers that stick to the top), and `PinnedHeaderSliver` / `SliverResizingHeader` in recent Flutter versions.

Only sliver widgets may go directly in `slivers:`; putting a plain widget there throws. Box widgets go inside `SliverToBoxAdapter`, and large lists must stay a `SliverList` to remain lazy — never a `Column` inside an adapter.

Slivers get **`SliverConstraints`** instead of width and height limits: how far the area has scrolled and how much of the screen is left to fill. They report back a `SliverGeometry`: how much space they take up and paint. That's what lets them shrink, stay pinned or disappear as you scroll.

`NestedScrollView` coordinates an outer header with scrolling areas inside it, for example tabs under a collapsing top bar.
takeaways: CustomScrollView combines several slivers in one scroll
SliverAppBar gives collapsing, pinned and floating headers
Only slivers go in `slivers:`; wrap box widgets in SliverToBoxAdapter
pitfalls: Putting a big Column of items in a SliverToBoxAdapter, losing lazy building.

quiz.q: You need a normal Text widget between a SliverAppBar and a SliverList. How do you add it?
options: Use a Column around all slivers
quiz.explain: slivers only accepts sliver widgets; SliverToBoxAdapter wraps a single box widget as a sliver.

concepts.name: Three trees and the rendering pipeline
concepts.summary: Understand widgets, elements and render objects, the build, layout and paint steps of every frame, and how Impeller turns them into pixels.
concepts.why: Fixing hard layout bugs and slow screens needs knowing exactly what happens between setState and pixels.
concepts.body:
Flutter keeps **three trees**:
- **Widgets** — immutable descriptions, rebuilt freely.
- **Elements** — the long-lived objects that hold the tree structure, State, and which inherited widgets each one depends on. `BuildContext` *is* the element.
- **Render objects** — do layout, painting and **hit testing** (working out which object a tap landed on). Only `RenderObjectWidget`s (like `Padding`, `Opacity`, `RichText`) create them; most widgets you write are combinations of other widgets and create none.

Each frame is made in a **pipeline** of steps, each feeding the next. The **Flutter engine** (the C++ core beneath the Dart code) signals when the screen is ready for a new frame (vsync), and `SchedulerBinding` runs:

1. **Animate** — tickers (per-frame timers) fire and animation controllers update their values.
2. **Build** — elements marked as needing a rebuild (by `setState` or a changed inherited widget) rebuild, top-down; elements are updated or replaced according to keys and types.
3. **Layout** — render objects marked `needsLayout` lay out: constraints down, sizes up. **Relayout boundaries** stop the work spreading upward when a parent's size can't depend on that child.

4. **Paint** — render objects record drawing commands into layers, separate sheets that are stacked into the final picture. `RepaintBoundary` gives a part of the tree its own layer so it can repaint alone.
5. **Composite** — the layers are assembled into one scene and handed to the engine.

6. **Rasterize** — on a separate **raster thread**, the scene becomes pixels on the **GPU** (the graphics chip). **Impeller**, the default renderer on iOS and Android, prepares its **shaders** (small GPU programs) when the app is built. That removes the stutter, or **jank**, that the older Skia renderer showed the first time an effect ran.

The UI thread (the **main thread**, which runs your Dart code) and the raster thread work at the same time, each with about 16 ms per frame at 60 frames a second (8 ms at 120). Flutter also builds a **semantics tree** from the render objects: a description of the screen for screen readers and other **accessibility** tools, which help people with disabilities use the app.
takeaways: Widgets describe, elements last, render objects lay out and paint
Frame = animate, build, layout, paint, composite, rasterize
Impeller prepares shaders in advance, avoiding first-run jank
pitfalls: Assuming a rebuild always means a repaint — unchanged render objects skip layout and paint.

quiz.q: In the three-tree model, which object is a BuildContext?
quiz.explain: BuildContext is the interface implemented by Element, representing the widget's location in the tree.

concepts.name: Profiling and performance
concepts.summary: Find and fix jank with profile mode and DevTools, reduce rebuilds, use const and RepaintBoundary, and avoid expensive effects.
concepts.why: Smooth 60–120 fps scrolling and animation is what users notice, and fixes require measuring first.
concepts.body:
Always measure in **profile mode** (`flutter run --profile`) on a real phone, ideally a cheap, slow one. Debug mode is much slower and misleading.

**DevTools** views:
- **Performance view** — a chart of frames, each split into UI-thread time (build, layout and paint in Dart) and raster time (drawing on the GPU). Red frames took longer than their time slot.
- **CPU profiler** — a **profiler** measures where time goes; this one shows which Dart functions take the most.
- **Track widget rebuilds** and "Highlight repaints" show unnecessary work.
- **Memory view** — finds objects that are never freed and large chunks of memory being reserved.

UI-thread fixes:
- Rebuild less: move state down the tree, split big widgets, use `const` constructors (identical const widgets are skipped), and `context.select` / `ValueListenableBuilder` to rebuild only what changed.
- Keep `build` cheap: never decode large downloaded data, sort big lists or read files in it. Move heavy calculations to an **isolate**, a separate Dart worker with its own memory that runs alongside the UI (`Isolate.run`).
- Use lazy builders for lists and grids; avoid `shrinkWrap` and intrinsic sizing (`IntrinsicHeight`), which force extra layout passes.

Raster-thread fixes:
- Avoid effects that make the GPU draw a part of the screen separately and then blend it in (Flutter calls this `saveLayer`): `Opacity` on large areas (use `FadeTransition` or a semi-transparent colour instead), `ShaderMask`, `ColorFilter`, and smooth-edged clipping on animated content.
- Wrap areas that repaint often (a spinner, a video) in `RepaintBoundary` so the rest isn't repainted.
- Size images to their display size with `cacheWidth`.

Check app size with `flutter build apk --analyze-size` and startup time with `--trace-startup`.
takeaways: Profile in profile mode on real devices with DevTools
Rebuild as little as possible: const widgets and narrow listeners
Avoid saveLayer-heavy effects; isolate repaints with RepaintBoundary
pitfalls: Optimizing blindly in debug mode without looking at the UI vs raster thread breakdown.

quiz.q: DevTools shows slow frames: the raster thread is over its time slot but the UI thread is fast. What's the most likely culprit?
options: Expensive painting effects such as Opacity or clips over large areas
quiz.explain: Raster time is GPU drawing work; effects that trigger saveLayer are a common cause, not Dart build work.

concepts.name: Platform channels, plugins and FFI
concepts.summary: Call native Android and iOS code with MethodChannel and EventChannel, generate type-safe bindings with Pigeon, and call C with dart:ffi.
concepts.why: When no ready-made plugin covers the phone feature or native library you need, you connect to Kotlin, Swift or C yourself.
concepts.body:
Your Dart code can't call Android or iOS features directly — the battery level, the camera, a payment company's SDK. Those are reached through **native code**: Kotlin or Java on Android, Swift or Objective-C on iOS, or C libraries, all compiled for the device itself. There are three ways in.

**Plugins** from pub.dev (`camera`, `url_launcher`, `shared_preferences`...) wrap native code behind a Dart API. Look for one first. Many are **federated**: split into one package per platform behind a shared Dart interface.

**Platform channels** pass asynchronous messages between your Dart code and the native app around it (the projects in `android/` and `ios/`):
- **`MethodChannel`** — request and response: Dart calls `await channel.invokeMethod<int>('getBattery')`; native code registers a handler and replies with a result or an error (which arrives as a `PlatformException`).
- **`EventChannel`** — a stream of events from native code to Dart (sensor readings, network on/off).

- Messages are encoded by `StandardMessageCodec`, which supports null, booleans, numbers, strings, lists of bytes (`Uint8List`), lists and maps.
- Native handlers run on the platform's **main thread** (the one that draws the screen) by default, so keep them quick. Move heavy work to a background task queue.

Channel names and arguments are plain strings, so a typo only shows up when the app runs. The Flutter team's **Pigeon** package generates matching, type-checked Dart, Kotlin and Swift code from one Dart interface definition.

**`dart:ffi`** (FFI, foreign function interface) calls C functions directly and **synchronously**: the call returns its result straight away instead of a future, with no messages in between. It's ideal for C libraries (SQLite, image decoders, encryption). `package:ffigen` generates the Dart bindings from C header files, and build hooks (native assets) can compile and bundle the C code. On iOS and macOS FFI can also reach Objective-C and Swift via `ffigen`, and Java/Kotlin via `jnigen` on Android.

Platform views (`AndroidView`, `UiKitView`) put a native view, such as a map, inside your Flutter screen, at some cost in speed.
takeaways: MethodChannel for request/response, EventChannel for native event streams
Use Pigeon for type-checked channels instead of hand-typed strings
dart:ffi calls C synchronously, without channels
pitfalls: Doing slow work in a native channel handler on the platform's main thread, freezing the app.

quiz.q: When is dart:ffi a better choice than a MethodChannel?
options: When calling a Kotlin screen API
When calling a C library directly and synchronously, without encoding messages
quiz.explain: FFI binds directly to C functions, avoiding asynchronous channel messages and their encoding.

concepts.name: CustomPainter and custom drawing
concepts.summary: Draw charts, gauges and custom shapes with CustomPaint and CustomPainter, repaint efficiently, and animate drawings.
concepts.why: When no widget fits the design, drawing on the canvas gives full control with excellent performance.
concepts.body:
**`CustomPaint`** hands you a **canvas** — a surface to draw on — through a **`CustomPainter`**:

- `paint(Canvas canvas, Size size)` draws with `canvas.drawLine`, `drawRect`, `drawRRect` (rounded rectangle), `drawCircle`, `drawArc`, `drawPath`, `drawImage`, and text via `TextPainter`. Coordinates start at the top-left corner of the given size.
- **`Paint`** objects describe the style: `color`, `strokeWidth`, `style` (filled or outline only), `strokeCap` (line ends), `shader` for **gradients** (colours that blend smoothly into each other), `maskFilter` for blur.
- **`Path`** builds complex shapes with `moveTo`, `lineTo`, smooth curves (`quadraticBezierTo`, `cubicTo`), `arcTo` and `addOval`, and can combine shapes with `Path.combine`.
- `canvas.save()` / `restore()` around `translate`, `rotate` and `scale` move or turn what you draw; `clipRect` / `clipPath` limit drawing to an area.

**`shouldRepaint(oldDelegate)`** decides whether a new painter needs to repaint; compare the inputs and return `false` when nothing changed.

For animation, pass the `Animation` (or any `Listenable`, an object that notifies listeners) as the painter's **`repaint`** argument: `MyPainter(progress: controller) : super(repaint: controller)`. The painter then repaints on every tick **without rebuilding any widgets** — the most efficient way to animate a drawing.

Give `CustomPaint` a size with `size:`, a child, or its parent's constraints; otherwise it may end up zero-sized. Wrap it in `RepaintBoundary` if it repaints often. To handle taps on custom shapes, override `hitTest`. For accessibility, provide `semanticsBuilder` or wrap it in `Semantics` with a label, since screen readers can't see what you drew.
takeaways: Draw with Canvas + Paint + Path in a CustomPainter
Pass an Animation as `repaint` to animate without rebuilding widgets
Implement `shouldRepaint` carefully and add semantics
pitfalls: Returning `true` from shouldRepaint unconditionally, repainting even when nothing changed.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of passing an AnimationController as a CustomPainter's `repaint` argument?
options: It caches the drawing as an image
The canvas repaints every tick without rebuilding the widget tree
quiz.explain: The painter listens to the Listenable and marks itself for repaint directly, skipping build and layout.
